Understanding simulation results

Turn an electron-normalized source spectrum into an energy-integrated yield and a physical photon rate, without confusing either with detector counts.

A source and its numerical sampling

This independently runnable example follows notebook 01. A 0.5 pC bunch at 100 kHz corresponds to 50 nA average beam current, regardless of how many Monte Carlo histories we sample. The low history counts below are chosen for teaching, not precision or convergence.

data.text/markdown:
Interpretation

result.to_dataframe() keeps each component's native energy grid. result.spectral_flux() forms a common grid by interpolation: "electron" returns source density, "sr" applies the physical electron rate, and "detector" also applies the accepted solid angle. Here the band integral intentionally uses CXR only, whereas the second plot includes all computed components. Integrating over energy removes the /eV dimension. These are expected emitted photon rates, not acquired counts: no exposure time, quantum efficiency, energy redistribution or Poisson counting has been applied. The scalar-detector acceptance uses a uniform-angular-density approximation. See the results how-to for saved checkpoints, and the model limitations and validation status before using a spectrum quantitatively. Try doubling bunch_charge_pc without changing histories: the electron-normalized yield stays the same, but the photon rate doubles. Then change the number of histories at fixed beam current to examine Monte Carlo variation. Continue to notebook 03 for ideal PXR line energies.
